pashtofolksong.basis: No source counts recordings. Discogs returns 136 hits for 'pashto' and 171 for 'pushto', most of them Pashto film-song 7-inch singles, a handful of Zarsanga and Gulnar Begum folk records, and Afghan field-recording LPs (Lyrichord 1971, Folkways 1977, Argo 1972, Traditional Crossroads 2003). The bulk of the genre sits on uncatalogued Peshawar cassettes (Odeon, Mehran and others from the early 1970s to about 2012), Radio Pakistan Peshawar and Radio Kabul tapes and Lok Virsa releases, so the true count is guessed from a cassette industry of many hundreds of singers each with dozens of tapes, of which a fraction is folk (tappa, charbeta, loba) rather than ghazal or film song. An insider's essential list would be about 40 performances (Zarsanga, Gulnar Begum, Kishwar Sultan, Mashooq Sultan, Hidayatullah, Khan Tehsil and classic tappa/charbeta singers).

bhawaiyaandbhatial.basis: No source counts recordings. Recording began on 78s in Kolkata in the 1930s–40s (Abbasuddin Ahmed for HMV, Megaphone, Twin and Regal; Kamala Jharia's 1934 bhatiali side), then decades of radio (Bangladesh Betar, All India Radio) and cassette releases on both sides of the border, and a large current stream of singles: an iTunes search finds 36 albums and singles titled 'bhawaiya' and 24 'bhatiali' (most since 2015), plus label series such as banglanatak's Bhawaiya and Bhatiyali VOL 1–3 (16–17 tracks each). One major folk singer, Abdul Alim, recorded about 500 songs across all folk forms. The canon an insider would name is a few dozen songs (oki gariyal bhai, fande pariya baga kande re, amay bhashaili re, etc.) in versions by Abbasuddin, his children, Rathindranath Roy and a handful of others.

hsaingwaing.basis: No source counts recordings. Discogs returns 36 hits for 'hsaing waing', of which about ten are releases of the ensemble itself: Folkways' 1950s Burmese survey, Ocora's 1981 'Birmanie: Musique d'art', the UNESCO/Auvidis disc (recorded 1977, issued 2001), Seven Seas' 1992 Tokyo session (reissued 2008), Kyaw Kyaw Naing's 1998 Shanachie album, Sublime Frequencies' nat pwe cassettes and a few untitled Burmese tapes. Behind them is a large, uncatalogued domestic cassette, VCD and radio output for zat pwe, anyeint, puppet and nat ensembles, the five types Burmese scholarship recognises, each with its own repertoire of tunes; the range is a judgement. Core: the theatre overtures, dance suites and best-known pieces a hsaing player would expect to know.

zapinandjoget.basis: No source counts recordings. Discogs text search finds 220 hits for zapin and 1359 for joget (the latter includes many dangdut and pop records named after the dance). From 1949 to the 1980s Malaysian and Singapore labels issued many joget singles and EPs and joget compilations of 14 singers (EMI Joget Pilihan, 1982); dance-music LPs (1974, 1978, 1983, 1990) label each track zapin, joget or inang. Indonesian Melayu zapin is mostly on local cassettes: Folkways notes no recordings from Sumatra or Riau were published outside Indonesia before its 1996 volume. An insider list would be about 40: the standard dance tunes (Serampang Laut, Hitam Manis, Kamarulzaman, Gambus Palembang, Lancang Kuning and similar) in a few versions each.

maracatu.basis: No source counts recordings. English Wikipedia gives around 20 nações in Recife and Olinda and dozens of rural groups; the Inventário Sonoro compilation alone has 19 nações. Albums found are mostly self-released CDs of 13-15 loas per group (Estrela Brilhante 2002, Leão Coroado 2004, Porto Rico 2004, Encanto da Alegria, Estrela Brilhante de Igarassu 2025), stage groups (Nação Pernambuco 1993, two LPs), rural-maracatu compilations (Maracatu Atômico, recorded 2000) and authors working from the tradition (Siba, Mestre Salustiano), plus composed carnival maracatus by Recife songwriters sung on record since the radio era, and hundreds of groups abroad. An insider's essential list is about 40 loas and performances.

currulao.basis: No source counts recordings. Known releases are small-label and festival-driven: Smithsonian Folkways (Grupo Naidy, 2005, 12 tracks; the group had two earlier CDs), Canalón de Timbiquí (four albums 2004–2019), Grupo Bahía/Hugo Candelario, Herencia de Timbiquí (four albums 2006–2014, fusion), Ecuadorian Esmeraldas marimba (Papá Roncón and others), plus the annual Petronio Álvarez festival in Cali (since 1996, with a marimba category) whose groups often self-release. Commercial recording seems to start in the 1970s (Pascual de Andagoya). Perhaps 100–300 albums of 10–14 tracks, many fusion; an insider's essential list is about 40 performances.

jota.basis: Aragon alone: the Fonoteca de la Jota in the Biblioteca de Aragón holds over 2,000 audio recordings (es.wikipedia); José Oto alone made about fifty discs; 78s by Miguel Asso, Jacinta Bartolomé, Pilar Gascón and others fill about three pages of the jota genre listing at UCLA's Strachwitz Frontera Collection; Jesús Gracia and the Pastor de Andorra recorded LPs from the 1950s to the 1990s. Beyond Aragon every Spanish region has its own jota, recorded in field anthologies (Lomax 1952, La tradición musical en España) and by revival groups since the 1970s (La Bullonera, Al Tall, Candeal, Hadit, La Musgaña, Eliseo Parra), each album carrying several jotas; MusicBrainz lists about 1,100 recordings with jota in the title, a fraction of the whole. Range is a reasoned guess, not a catalogue count; core is what an Aragonese listener would call essential, plus the main regional and revival recordings.

hardangerfiddleand.basis: No catalogue counts recordings. The repertoire is over 1000 registered slåttar for the Hardanger fiddle plus variants, 400 of them from Telemark (Norwegian Wikipedia, Hardingfele). Commercial output runs from 78s by the 1920s (Halvor Bråthen, 1928) through solo albums of 14-26 tunes each by players such as Knut Buen, Hauk Buen, the Bjørgums, Knut Hamre (12 albums), Benedicte Maurseth and Annbjørg Lien on Heilo, Grappa, Sylvartun and Etnisk Musikklubb, plus Ocora and archive series. Recordings of tunes on releases are estimated at a few thousand; archive tapes (Norsk folkemusikksamling) would add more. Core is what a player would call the essential tunes and performances across Telemark, Setesdal, Hardanger, Voss, Valdres and Hallingdal.
